title: How to Use the Non-Freaked Out Framework for Personal PD: A Case Study
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart argues that professional development for teachers is overwhelming and incoherent, and that his six-part Non-Freaked Out Framework works as a filter for personal growth as well as classroom focus. He lists five benefits: it organizes incoming information, aids retention, exposes the opportunity cost of each thing learned, lets him satisfice mandatory PD, and supports focused self-designed studies. He then offers a case study of a three-week research sprint on noncognitive factors: three short books, fifteen articles pulled from their reference lists at five per week, and a follow-up writing sprint. The articles proved more productive than the books, notably surfacing Farrington's report. He concludes that picking one topic and diving deep was liberating and fruitful, while noting that this is an example and not a prescription.
points: A personal framework is a PD filter: it gives new studies a place to live, which helps retention and reduces overwhelm.
Every PD choice has an opportunity cost, so Stuart declines to chase edu-tech or project-based learning until his core framework is mastered.
The framework tells him which mandatory PD to learn effortfully and which to learn only enough to pass.
His research-sprint design, books first and then references from the books, shows how to go deep on one topic in a few weeks.
Writing about what he learns is both a learning tool and a motivator, so he follows reading sprints with writing sprints.
quotes: The array of professional development resources available to teachers today is as overwhelming as it is incoherent. Every month, dozens of books and hundreds of articles and thousands of tweets are published. Yet for most of us, this overabundance is more a source of stress or apathy than it is a source of professional growth.
It coheres the noise. If Insert Guru Here shares a new study about reading or literacy, the NFO Framework gives me a place to put it.

It helps me see the opportunity cost of everything I learn. Every new bit of professional development I take in comes at a cost — while I was learning about the expectancy-value theory of motivation yesterday afternoon, I wasn’t learning about the latest edu-tech website.

It helps me satisfice mandatory PD. There are, of course, things I’m required to learn to keep my job — e.g., the teacher evaluation model my district uses, or how the latest data warehouse software works.

While reading the books, I made note of anything listed in their reference sections that I wanted to read further, and I selected five of these references to read each week. Because the Wooden book had no references, I saved it for last and read five references from the other books during the week that I was reading Wooden.

I’m a big fan of this approach, both because it was enjoyable and because it was fruitful. Giving myself permission to stick with one topic (noncognitive factors) and dive deep into it was both liberating and powerful.
However, the writing continues, and this post is a part of it. Writing about what I learn is (as you know) a chief means through which I deepen that learning, not to mention a big motivator.
